about: Quick checks for the questions that come up most about IRL streaming, written as checks along the chain: camera and mic, sender, connections, receiver, OBS, platform. Fields: id (an anchor), question, summary (which part most likely broke), checks (1 to 3; each has short plain text and optionally the part it looks at; no product names or product settings), words (ids in words.json), services (ids in services.json whose own docs and support channels help with the question), sources (the primary docs behind the checks; at least one required). Product specifics live in guides.json and services.json, never in the checks. Our own words only; no community posts quoted or linked. Validated by the zod schema in ../schema.

answers.question: My app says I'm live, but the platform shows me offline
answers.summary: Your app may send to a hub: a cloud OBS, a relay with drop protection or OBS at home. The hub goes live on the platform with its own Start.

checks.text: Check where your app sends. If it's a hub, live in the app only means the hub is receiving.
Start the hub's output: Start Streaming in OBS, or the start button or command of your cloud service.
Check that a destination is added and switched on, and watch the platform's dashboard during a test.

answers.question: How do I get a steady feed into OBS?
answers.summary: OBS takes one finished stream. With bonding, a receiver joins the connections back together first, and OBS reads from the receiver.

checks.text: Put a receiver between your connections and OBS; OBS can't join bonded connections by itself.
Point the OBS source at the receiver's address, not at the phone or box.
Let a scene switcher show your BRB scene when the feed drops, and switch back when it returns.

answers.question: OBS shows my video, but the scene switcher sees no numbers
answers.summary: The picture and the numbers take different roads. OBS plays the stream from one address; the switcher reads the receiver's stats from another.

checks.text: Give the switcher the receiver's stats address, not the one OBS plays. A switcher in the cloud needs a public address.
Set the server type to the software that runs your receiver, not to the app or box that sends.
Let one automatic switcher control each OBS; two switchers fight each other.

answers.question: The switcher went back to LIVE, but the picture is frozen
answers.summary: A scene switcher only changes scenes. The OBS source that plays your feed has to reconnect too, and not every source does that by itself.

checks.text: Look at the receiver's numbers. If the feed arrives, the source in OBS is what's stuck.
Reconnect the source: refresh it in OBS, or use your switcher's fix-feed command if it has one.
Use a source made for live feeds over weak networks; it reconnects by itself after a dropout.

answers.question: My second connection is connected, but the stream doesn't use it
answers.summary: Connected isn't the same as carrying. Either the sender isn't bonding over it, or that connection can't reach the receiver.

checks.text: Check that bonding is on in the sender and that it lists every connection.
Run a short test and watch each connection's traffic. Zero on one means it isn't helping yet.
Check that the receiver can be reached over that connection: turn any VPN off, and keep a spare phone awake.

answers.question: The camera picture froze or stutters, but I'm still live
answers.summary: Find where it starts. If the preview on your phone or box already freezes, the break is between the camera and the sender, not the internet.

checks.text: Look at the preview on your phone or box. If it already freezes or stutters there, the camera's link is the cause.
Check that link: cable and capture card seated, or Wi-Fi close by and on 5 GHz if it can.
Preview smooth? Look at the bitrate going out. If that drops, the connections are the cause.

answers.question: My Wi-Fi camera connects, but the app's preview stays black
answers.summary: Two causes look the same: the camera sends to the wrong address, or the app isn't allowed to use the camera or microphone. Check one at a time.

checks.text: Compare the address the camera sends to with the one your app shows. It must be the phone's own address, never 0.0.0.0.
Allow the app to use the camera and microphone in the phone's settings, even for a Wi-Fi camera.
Restart the camera's live mode after each change.

answers.question: The sound is missing, on the wrong mic or drifting
answers.summary: If the picture is fine but the sound isn't, follow the sound from the mic: the input, then the sender, then OBS.

checks.text: Check the mic is plugged in and chosen as the input, and that its level moves when you speak.
Check which mic the sender uses in each scene; some senders change the mic when the scene changes.
Crackles or drifts after a dropout? Look at the OBS source taking the feed; a source made for IRL recovers by itself.

answers.question: Switching cameras drops the stream, or the platform shows black
answers.summary: The platform is refusing what arrives after the switch. Find out whether it's one camera or every switch, then compare with what the platform asks for.

checks.text: Switch to each camera on its own. If only one causes it, compare its resolution and frame rate with the others.
Compare your encoder settings with the platform's own recommended settings page.
Change one thing at a time, and test each change with a short stream.

answers.question: My cloud destination keeps switching itself off
answers.summary: When the platform refuses the connection, a cloud OBS stops retrying and switches the destination off. Fix the reason, then switch it back on.

checks.text: Changed your stream key or password? Link the platform account again, or paste the new key.
Stop any other device that streams with the same key.
On a custom destination, turn authentication off unless the platform asks for it. Then switch it back on.
